content: Ergot is a fungus belonging to the genus Claviceps, which parasitizes certain grains and grasses. The overwintering form of this fungus is called a sclerotium, a small, hardened structure commonly referred to as ergot. While the term ergot is often used to describe the sclerotium, it is also correct to use it to refer to members of the Claviceps genus. There are approximately 50 known species of Claviceps, most of which are found in tropical regions. Economically significant species include Claviceps purpurea (which parasitizes grasses and cereals), C. fusiformis (affecting pearl millet and buffel grass), C. paspali (on dallis grass), and C. africana. Among these, C. purpurea is particularly notable for its ability to infect various cereals, including rye (its most common host), triticale, wheat, and barley, though it rarely affects oats. Claviceps purpurea has three distinct varieties based on host specificity: G1: Found on grasses in open meadows and fields. G2: Found on grasses in moist, forested, or mountainous habitats. G3 (C. purpurea var. spartinae): Found on salt marsh grasses such as Spartina and Distichlis. Life Cycle of the Fungus The ergot sclerotium develops when a flowering grass or cereal floret is infected by a spore of the Claviceps fungus. The infection process mimics the growth of a pollen grain into an ovary during fertilization. The fungus destroys the plant ovary and attaches itself to a vascular bundle meant for seed nutrition. The initial stage of infection produces a white, soft tissue called sphacelia, which secretes a sugary substance known as honeydew. This honeydew contains millions of asexual spores (conidia) that are dispersed to other florets by insects. Over time, the sphacelia transforms into a hard, dry sclerotium within the husk of the floret. At this stage, the sclerotium accumulates alkaloids and lipids. In tropical and subtropical Claviceps species, the honeydew contains both macroconidia and microconidia. Macroconidia vary in shape and size between species, while microconidia are uniform, oval to globose in shape (5 x 3 μm). Macroconidia can produce secondary conidia. A germ tube emerges from a macroconidium through the surface of a honeydew droplet, forming a secondary conidium of an oval to pear-like shape, which contains the contents of the original macroconidium. These secondary conidia form a frost-like surface on honeydew droplets and are dispersed by wind. However, this process does not occur in Claviceps purpurea, C. grohii, C. nigricans, or C. zizaniae, all of which are found in temperate regions. When a mature sclerotium falls to the ground, the fungus remains dormant until favorable conditions, such as the onset of spring or a rainy period, trigger its fruiting phase. The sclerotium germinates, producing one or more fruiting bodies with a head and stipe, resembling tiny mushrooms. In the head, threadlike sexual spores are formed and ejected simultaneously when suitable grass hosts are flowering. Ergot infection reduces the yield and quality of grain and hay. If infected grain or hay is consumed by livestock, it can cause a disease known as ergotism. The black, protruding sclerotia of C. purpurea are well-known, but many tropical ergots have brown or grayish sclerotia that mimic the shape of the host seed, making the infection easy to overlook. Effects on Humans and Animals The ergot sclerotium contains high concentrations (up to 2% of dry mass) of ergotamine, a complex molecule composed of a tripeptide-derived cyclol-lactam ring linked to a lysergic acid (ergoline) moiety, along with other alkaloids of the ergoline group biosynthesized by the fungus. Ergot alkaloids exhibit a wide range of biological activities, including effects on circulation and neurotransmission. Ergotism refers to severe pathological syndromes in humans or animals caused by the ingestion of ergot alkaloid-containing plant material, such as ergot-contaminated grains. Historically, ergotism was known as St. Anthony's fire due to symptoms like severe burning sensations in the limbs, caused by vasoconstriction of blood vessels. In extreme cases, this vasoconstriction can lead to gangrene and limb loss due to restricted blood circulation. The neurotropic effects of ergot alkaloids can also cause hallucinations, irrational behavior, convulsions, and even death. Other symptoms include strong uterine contractions, nausea, seizures, and unconsciousness. Monks of the Order of St. Anthony the Great specialized in treating ergotism victims using balms containing tranquilizing and blood circulation-stimulating plants. They were also skilled in performing amputations. In addition to ergot alkaloids, Claviceps paspali produces tremorgens (paspalitrem) that cause paspalum staggers in cattle. Ergot alkaloids are also produced by fungi of the genera Penicillium and Aspergillus, notably by some isolates of the human pathogen Aspergillus fumigatus. These alkaloids have also been isolated from plants in the family Convolvulaceae, such as morning glory. Historically, controlled doses of ergot were used to induce abortions and to stop maternal bleeding after childbirth, but simple ergot extracts are no longer used pharmaceutically. Ergot does not contain lysergic acid diethylamide (LSD) but contains ergotamine, which is used to synthesize lysergic acid, a precursor for LSD synthesis. Lysergic acid can be isolated from ergot. A 2007 study published in the New England Journal of Medicine documented that two Parkinson's disease drugs derived from ergot, pergolide and cabergoline, may increase the risk of leaky heart valves by up to 700%. Historical and Speculative Context The disease cycle of the ergot fungus was first described in the 1800s, but its connection to epidemics among humans and animals was known centuries earlier. Human poisoning from consuming rye bread made from ergot-infected grain was common in medieval Europe, where it was referred to as St. Anthony's Fire or ignis sacer. Speculatively, it has been suggested that the Salem witch trials were initiated by young women who consumed ergot-tainted rye. Some historians have also linked the Great Fear during the French Revolution to the influence of ergot. British author John Grigsby has proposed that ergot was used as a ritual drink in prehistoric fertility cults, similar to the Eleusinian Mysteries in ancient Greece. He argues that the Anglo-Saxon poem Beowulf may reference the suppression of such a fertility cult, with Beowulf (meaning barley-wolf) suggesting a connection to ergot, which was known in German as the tooth of the wolf. Poisonings from seeds treated with mercury compounds are sometimes misidentified as ergotism. For example, the mass poisoning in Pont-Saint-Esprit, France, in 1951 was initially attributed to ergotism but was later found to be caused by a toxic mercury compound used to disinfect grain. Similar outbreaks occurred in Iraq (1956, 1960, and 1971–72), West Pakistan (1961), and Guatemala (1965), often due to the consumption of treated seed grains. In the case of the 1971–72 Iraq epidemic, grain treated with methyl mercury fungicide was mistakenly used for food, resulting in 459 deaths. The grain had been dyed red and labeled with warnings in English and Spanish, which were not understood by the local population. The beverage kykeon, consumed during the ancient Greek Eleusinian Mysteries, may have been based on hallucinogens derived from ergot. Today, rye grain is deliberately infected to produce ergot for research and pharmaceutical purposes.
